name: Dating-profile photo optimization

lead: This is picking, editing and ordering your dating-app photos using outside feedback rather than your own preference, so the strongest shots lead your profile.

It is most often done with Photofeeler, where anonymous voters rate photos on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness. Supporters say outside ratings show how strangers see a photo, since friends and family may be overly kind. Forum members report mixed results, including top-rated photos that did not do best on apps.

paras: People upload candidate photos to a rating site, compare scores and comments, then choose and order the best ones for their profile. Results come back within hours to a day or so.
Low physical risk. Reported drawbacks include raters favouring smiling expressions, discouraging scores, and sharing photos with strangers.

angle.text: Rating candidate photos with anonymous voters lets you select and order the shots that come across best on a dating profile. Users value the outside view, though forum members report that top-rated photos do not always perform best on apps.

lead: Dating-profile photo optimization is the practice of selecting, editing and ordering photographs for dating apps using feedback or data, rather than personal preference alone. In looksmaxxing communities it is most often associated with Photofeeler, a site where anonymous voters rate photos on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness.[1][2]

Proponents say outside ratings reveal how strangers perceive a photo, since friends and family may give overly positive opinions.[2] Forum members also report cases where rated-highest photos did poorly on dating apps, and criticism that raters favour smiling expressions.
No independent studies were found testing whether Photofeeler-optimised photos increase dating-app matches.

paras: The practice involves choosing which photos to use on a dating profile, and in what order, by testing them with strangers. Photofeeler's dating test asks voters to rate a photo on smartness, trustworthiness and attractiveness.[1] Grokipedia says the site's founders wanted objective feedback because friends and family tend to be overly positive.[2]

Photofeeler reports scores adjusted for voter tendencies and standardised within gender and age groups, and offers comments from voters.[2] The company has published analyses of its own data, including a 2014 study of business photos and a 2019 neural network paper trained on 1.2 million dating photos.[1]

Members of looksmax.org share Photofeeler scores and debate their usefulness. Reported complaints include a mismatch between rater scores and Tinder results and a perceived bias toward smiling photos. Others compare results across voter-age and gender settings.

lore.intro: Photofeeler is the main reference point; forum members dispute how well its scores predict dating-app performance.

claims.claim: Rated-best photos do not necessarily perform best on dating apps
